Messages.Author: Sigmund Bjornstein
Messages.Body:
Greetings.

All right,let's take a highly hypothetical situation (not related to
anything that has ever actually happened, mind). Let's say I'm playing
a Gangrel rush deck; Badger is sending a vampire to torpor, but
diablerizes with Amaranth instead. A blood hunt is called (of course).
It happens that the winning votes belong to a player across the table,
neither my predator nor my prey.

May I ask him to vote against the blood hunt:

a) Pretty please, with sugar on top?
b) And I promise to pay him back by rushing his predator (or his
prey)?
c) Or else I'll rush _him_ next, and see how he likes it?
d) And I promise that Gitane St Claire will lend her vote to all his
political actions?
e) None of the above?

It has been argued that this sort of dealing in the middle of a vote
is not allowed, since that's what the Succubus Club is for. How about
that, is that true?

Thanks,

-- Sigmund

Messages.Body:

> May I ask him to vote against the blood hunt:

Yes.

> a) Pretty please, with sugar on top?
> b) And I promise to pay him back by rushing his predator (or his
> prey)?
> c) Or else I'll rush _him_ next, and see how he likes it?
> d) And I promise that Gitane St Claire will lend her vote to all his
> political actions?
> e) None of the above?

Any of the above (except e). Note that none of the terms specified
are enforced by the rules - you are free to break your promises.

> It has been argued that this sort of dealing in the middle of a vote
> is not allowed, since that's what the Succubus Club is for. How about
> that, is that true?

Neither the Succubus Club nor the absense of the Succubus Club has
any effect on the ability to table talk.

Succubus Club adds the ability to make a few types of immediate
trades (something for something right now - no future concerns),
that's all. (card text).

You are always free to make promises. You are also not bound to
keep those.

Messages.Author: Andrew S. Davidson
Messages.Body:
On 1 Feb 2002 11:33:56 -0800, Sigmund Bjornstein wrote:

>It has been argued that this sort of dealing in the middle of a vote
>is not allowed, since that's what the Succubus Club is for. How about
>that, is that true?

Yes.

In addition to the point you make, note that the player with the
casting vote only has 15 seconds in which to do so. Players who tried
to offer inducements, threats, counter-threats and so forth would
disrupt the voting process. You'd get everyone trying to speak at
once and it might not be clear whether the vote was actually cast
during the hubbub.

In the real world there are laws against this sort of thing. I've
spent much time shivering outside polling stations because political
representatives are not allowed inside to twist voters arms. And
offering bribes and inducements is right out. But, as this is the
World of Darkness and set in cities like Chicago and Miami, the game
provides cards for players who want to indulge in such shenanigans. If
you want other players to vote your way then you use cards like
Bribes, Telepathic Vote Counting and Charming Lobby. But creating
your own DIY game effects is not allowed. This is not the RPG or
LARP; it's a card game.

Andrew

On 04 Feb 2002 23:31:48 GMT, Halcyan 2 wrote:

>Please ignore Andrew. He likes to stir up trouble from time to time by
>pretending he doesn't understand the rules

There's no rule to understand here. There are no rules for
negotiations, deals, threats, propaganda, etc. That's why, if you're
playing the game strictly, they are not allowed.

LSJ appears to have some personal rules for this but hasn't troubled
to put them in the rulebook and therefore, so far as the official game
is concerned, they don't exist.

You will, of course, find that in practise judges will tell you that
you can or can't do certain things. For example, if you whisper or
gesticulate to another player, this may or may not be allowed. But
this has no basis in the rules - they just make this stuff up
according to their personal taste. Their taste usually seems to be an
environment of honest dealing - where players make open public deals
and always keep their word. This is wildly inappropriate for Vampire
because:

a) the World of Darkness background is one of inhuman monsters, secret
conspiracies and Machiavellian intrigue. There are no good guys in
this world - even the Society of Leopold is corrupt. Trading on your
real-world, personal reputation rather than adopting the role of an
evil Methusaleh destroys the role-playing feel of the game - an
important element of the design.

b) the game's designer, Richard Garfield, made it clear that he didn't
want player interaction to be the stereotyped
whining/finger-pointing/bash-the-leader dynamic which would reduce a
multi-player game to a simple model, just as NCL focussed decks reduce
the game to rock/scissors/paper. He analysed these outcomes in
another article which I should perhaps reproduce. Vampire was
supposed to solve this by forcing players to concentrate upon ousting
their prey. Binding deals are often used to subvert this design aim
and so they are not just ultra vires, they are actually bad for the
game.

Andrew

Secret dealing is frowned on or disallowed in tournaments because of

accomodate the time-outs required.

interactions that are kept from the Judge and the other players at the
table. Deal breaking is permitted and even encouraged by most judges,
at least in my experience. At my last tournament, the Judge
practically advised a player that it was his duty to break a deal
because he could thereby gain a victory point. The concern is that
one is supposed to play to win, and to do otherwise is thought to
stink of "collusion".

Some players choose to keep deals, others don't. I say, let there be
variety.

Few players make a rule of always keeping deals (but some do, and this
is allowed), but most good players usually keep deals and make
exceptions only in high-stakes situations. This does not make them
saintly, just a bit more sophisticated at "Machiavellian intrigue"
than the average Sabbat !Brujah neonate sadist thug.

> b) the game's designer, Richard Garfield, made it clear that he didn't
> want player interaction to be the stereotyped

I believe we are now discussing apples and oranges. Deal breaking and
deal making is very much a part of a wide variety of multiplayer
games. I don't think it was this that Garfield sought to minimize,
but rather the tendency of players in multiplayer games to gang up on
and destroy the stronger player because he is considered a threat.

On 5 Feb 2002 06:18:56 -0800, John B. Whelan wrote:

>This does not follow. If there are no rules against something, then
>the typical default assumption is that it is allowed.

That's true of live action games like LARP, paintball etc. That's
because you have the laws of the real world to constrain you - both
legal and physical. This doesn't work in board and card games because

Andrew Davidson wrote:

>I recall your incredulity when I put forward the proposition that a

Then you recall something that I do not. When have we had previous debate? I
suspect you mistake me for someone else, or else this was very long ago.

I don't. I was merely reporting the attitude of the Judge about how he
personally felt the game should be played. (He was not, BTW, making a
ruling. He had no authority to do so as he was playing in the game himself
under the multi-Judge system. He was merely expressing an opinion on how folks
should play.)

I believe that the only circumstances in which a person should be "required to
break a deal" is if the original deal was itself illegal .. ie. was originally
motivated by some other reason than attempting to win. But if the original
deal was made in the proper spirit, then a player should not be required to
break it just because he finds it no longer in his interest.

Players should not be required to keep deals, but neither should they be forced
to break them.

Last time I checked, this was still the official position.

> That's mainly what I'm after - a general acceptance
>that players should always act in their own interest and break deals
>when they are no longer useful - helping another player more than they
>help themselves.

General game theory suggests that while deal-breakers do well in the short run,
they tend to do worse in the long run. And the longer the "long run" is, the
worse the idea of deal-breaking becomes.

If the "Eternal Struggle" were truly eternal (and in a sense it is, because the
Methuselahs are always returning to the table) then it may well be that
deal-breaking is never a good idea.

But if one is going to break a deal, it makes sense to do so when the stakes
are high. For instance, a smart Methuselah might always keep his word ...
except in the final round of tournament with a hefty prize. Or he might only
break his word when it is given to strangers whom he does not expect to play
again with any regularity.

But my attitude is ... the stakes are NEVER high. It's just a card game, and
the most I ever got for participating in a Tournament was a $100.00 box of
cards. Poor as I am, that is still small potatoes in the ultimate scheme of
things, and hardly worth sacrificing the value of my given word.

If it is ever decreed that players MUST break deals, I'll simply stop making
them. Deal making is only valuable if people trust you anyway, so there is
hardly much point if there is "general acceptance" that deals must be broken.
If one's word is worthless, then there is nothing it can buy.

Of course, me and my playgroup can play with the understanding that deals
should be broken. I this case, I can make a promise, and the recipient of the
promise will know I don't really mean it, and I will know he knows this, and
therefore, in effect, it is not really a promise at all, and my integrity is in
no way affected when I break the (essentially non-existent) deal.

I won't say there is NO point to the above situation. Essentially they have
agreed to play a game of bluff where each tries to guess when the other is
lying. It also has the advantage of reducing the amount of promise-making
deals (since there is no longer any point to them), which is good if you do not
like the deal-making aspect of the game. But the "bluff" aspect will apply
only to lies about current game information (like what is in your hand or
deck), since promises will be dismissed as irrelevant.

But if you really want to play the roll of an "evil" Methuselah who breaks his
promises, then you will not get anywhere unless you actually fool someone into
trusting you. This is impossible under the "general acceptance" system you
advocate. In order to be fooled by an "evil" Methuselah whe breaks his
promises, one must believe, at least hypothetically, in a "good" Methuselah who
does not break them -- which cannot be if the latter is actually outlawed
(except to the extent that one's victims are ignorant of the rules).

It is the very nature of evil that it must prey on good to gain any advantage.
Treachery, to be valuable, must prey on trust. If you outlaw good, there is
nothing for Evil to take advantage of, and no possibility of Treachery.
If you really think that Treachery is an important aspect of the game (and I
agree with you that it is), then it would be a bad thing if you were to obtain
the general acceptance that you advocate. The game should have at least some
honest Methuselahs who mean what they say and follow through on their word.

If honest folk did not exist, then confidence men would be out of work. It is
not necessary that the victims be honest, but it is necessary that victims
believe in the possibility of honesty in others. I fancy that the con-men in
Hell do very poor business.

-- John Whelan

> On 5 Feb 2002 06:18:56 -0800, John B. Whelan wrote:

>
> Really? I've heard more than one UK player say words to the effect

> wouldn't bleed his prey when he had left himself wide open.

I was another of those who came out with that statement at Saturday's
event - I know that Ross (Howard, who also attended the game) thinks
similarly. As a personal rule, I don't tend to break in-game
agreements (I can't recall having done so to date), though I will
stick to the letter of them - for instance, I cut a deal with Jackie
not to bleed her on my next turn in order to secure her support for a
vote, then hit her with a Kine Resources Contested instead (I would
also have considered redirecting a bleed to her acceptable under the
terms of the agreement). I accept that many players will break a deal
if it is beneficial for them, but I hold the view that people will be
more likely to take up your deals if they believe you will abide by
them (e.g. you have a good reputation for sticking to your deals) - I
believe one of the tips on the ELDB is something along the lines of
'never expect a dealbreaker to keep to their deals'?

Whilst it is arguably using knowledge from outside the immediate game,
could anyone say that they cwould be able to weigh up whether to
accept a deal offered by someone that they know has a record of
breaking deals without that knowledge affecting their decision
(compared to someone they know has a reputation for holding to a deal,
even if it costs them)?

Whilst (by the tournament rules) you must play with the aim of
obtaining a game win, and of course you should not accept a deal that
will detriment you without a benefit which outweighs such in terms of
advancing your chances of securing a game win (e.g. voting for a
referendum that disadvantages you in order to secure someone else's
votes for your next political action would, I think, be acceptable in
the majority of player's minds), surely this would not force you to
break a deal if the situation changed? Dealmaking is a key part of
the game - to force someone to break a deal (rather than giving them
the option to) is, in my opinion, a bad idea. In other words, take
the following situations:

i) Player A cuts a deal with player B, their prey, to not bleed him
on the next turn in return for them rushing and taking out the nasty,
killer minion of Player C, A's predator, a vampire which is causing A
extreme problems for some reason (perhaps they have +1 innate stealth,
or are a combat monster who keeps knocking A's minions into torpor,
whatever). B successfully does so and taps out. It comes around to
A's turn, and A realises he could now bleed B out.

ii) Same situation, but player A gets bled badly by C before it rolls
around to his turn again, and if he does not bleed out player B, it is
99% certain he will be ousted by C on C's next turn - the six pool
could save him...

Certainly A could decide to break the deal, but in either case would
the current tournament rules force player A to break the deal, even if
they would prefer to choose not to (even at the cost of being ousted
next turn)? In my opinion, as when the deal was cut it was done with
the aim of furthering A's position, they should have the option of
sticking to it even though it could now cost them.

Opinions/rulings? Can this tournament rule force you to break a deal
made in good faith against your wishes?

- Rafe

See, my attitude is that your given word doesn't
*have* much value within a game of VTES. Since it's
only a game, and treachery is (IMO) part of that game,

expect to gain something by doing so (eg the ability
to make further deals with that player during that
game).

Right. Players should only be willing to work together
in a game of VTES when it's actually to *both* of their
advantages to do so. If word-keeping is required for
both of them to benefit, it's generally not a deal that
should be made. (again, IMO.)

> If honest folk did not exist, then confidence men would be out of work.
It is
> not necessary that the victims be honest, but it is necessary that victims
> believe in the possibility of honesty in others. I fancy that the con-men
in
> Hell do very poor business.

I'd actually like to see con-men do poor business in
VTES too. I don't like people getting jedi-mind-tricked
into doing stupid things to another player's benefit,
or bamboozled into thinking somebody's going to keep a
deal that won't be to the other person's benefit once
they've fulfilled their end of the bargain. I think
the game would work better if everyone recognized that
it's only in any other player's interest to help you
as long as it helps them too, and therefore not expect
help (or deals to be kept) beyond that point.

As in some cases in the "real world", if you're not
bargaining from a position of strength, you're not
bargaining at all, you're just begging for mercy.

No.

A contrived (not exactly real-world) example built to conform
to the following scenario: Two players have the opportunity to
cooperate (keep the deal) or defect (break the deal) - with the
decision being made simultaneously.

If both coopoerate, they score 3 point each on some reward scale.
If both defect, then score 1 point each.
If one defects and the other cooperates, the defector gets 5 points
and the other gets 0.

In an isolated "game" of the above, you should always defect.
You will invariably score better that way.

The game gets interesting when iterated and applied (pairwise)
to larger groups. In that case (with suitable set-up conditions),
it is better to cooperate with a given partner upon the initial
meeting, and then in each subsequent meeting, to choose the
action that was the partner last chose (the "Tit-for-tat"
algorithm.

> that long-term "cooperation" (ie cross-game, even beyond
> a certain point in-game) is already prohibited by VEKN

Interesting. And thanks for the links. It does seem

very analogous to VTES deals (at least the ones I've
seen). For one thing, in VTES it's not really feasible
to cooperate for the entire game with another player.
(One of you has to get ousted for the game to end,
barring a mutual-withdrawal pact, and even then you're
still competing to win the game.) That is, there are
(IMO) no deals in VTES that in the long-term can be
good for everybody (though there may be some in the
short term). Or, my take is that the payoffs in VTES
are such that cooperating every time (or playing the
tit-for-tat strategy) is not a recipe for winning.

If, for example, player A offers player B, his prey,
a deal that A won't oust B on his next turn, in
return for B using his Bum's Rushes on his own prey
instead of on A, it's then in A's interest (once B
doesn't rush him) to go ahead and oust B anyway (if
it's in his power to do so). The ability to have
B trust him in the future will almost certainly not
pay off in an amount greater than the 1 VP that
defecting gets him now. (This is because generally
it's almost never going to be in B's interest to
outright help A gain VPs in the future. The deals
it will be in B's interest to make may have some
benefits to A, but as far as I can see, not generally
anything large enough to outweigh a VP.)

This is still not to say that A couldn't keep the
deal and not oust B. It's just that in my opinion,
it's almost never *truly* worthwhile for him to do
so. The downside of being known as a "dealbreaker"
under those circumstances doesn't outweigh getting
even a single VP - being known as a "dealkeeper"
will never actually gain you VPs unless people are
outright paying you back for favors you've done
them in other games - and that I do think is not
legal under VEKN tournament rules.

The typical VTES deal is an asymmetric game because the players take
their actions openly and sequentially. For the player who goes first
it's a stag hunt because the payoff for defection is not greater than
the payoff for mutual cooperation. For the player who goes second,
it's a degenerate form of the prisoner's dilemma because defecting is
a no-brainer when you can already see that the other player has
cooperated.

The general situation is additionally complicated because the players
also have the option of dealing with other players or not dealing at
all and so there are usually more than two choices.

I like the following analysis of the simple situation which comes from
The Prisoner's Dilemma by William Poundstone.

Andrew

------------------------------------------------------------------

"In 1966, Melvin J. Guyer and Anatol Rapoport, then both at the
University of Michigan, catalogued all the simple games. The simplest
true games have two players making a choice between two alternatives.
It is reasonable to think that these "2 x 2" games ought to be
particularly important and common. The prisoner's dilemma and chicken
are 2 x 2 games, of course. There are seventy-eight distinct 2 x 2
games when payoffs are simply ranked rather than assigned numerical
values.

A symmetric game is one where the payoffs are the same for each player
under comparable circumstances - where neither player is in a
privileged position. If player A is the lone cooperator, his payoff is
the same as player B's would be if he was the lone cooperator, and so
forth. Symmetric games are the easiest to understand, and probably the
most important in social interactions. People are much the same the
world over. No conflicts are so common or so bitter as those between
people wanting the same thing. So let's look at the symmetric games.

There are just four payoffs to worry about in a symmetric 2 x 2 game.
Let "CC" be the payoff, to each of the two players, when both
cooperate. "DD" is the payoff when both defect. When one player
cooperates and the other defects, the payoff to the lone cooperator
will be called "CD," and the payoff to the lone defector, "DC."

All the variety of 2 x 2 symmetric games rests in the relative values
of the four payoffs CC, DD, CD, and DC. As usual, let's have the
players rank them in order of preference (and they must agree on the
ranking, it being a symmetric game). Let's further assume that there
are no "ties," that there is always a distinct preference between any
two payoffs.

Any given preference ordering of the four payoffs defines a game. For
instance, when

DC>CC>DD>CD

- meaning that the DC outcome is preferred to CC, which is preferred
to DD, which is preferred to CD - the game is a prisoner's dilemma.
(The usual further requirement, that the average of the DC and CD
payoffs be less than the CC payoff, applies only when players hare
assigned numerical values to the payoffs. Here we're just ranking
them.)

There are twenty-four possible rankings of four payoffs, and thus
twenty-four symmetric 2 x 2 games. Not all are dilemmas. In most, the
correct strategy is obvious.

The disturbing thing about the prisoner's dilemma and chicken is the
way that the common good is subverted by individual rationality. Each
player desires the other's cooperation, yet is tempted to defect
himself.

Let's see what this means in general terms. The payoff CC must be
preferred to CD. That means that you're better off when your partner
returns your cooperation. Also, DC must be better than DD. You still
hope the other player cooperates, even when you yourself defect.

Of the twenty-four possible orderings of four payoffs, exactly half
have the CC payoff higher than the CD payoff. Likewise, exactly half
have DC preferred to DD. Just six of the possible orderings
simultaneously meet both requirements. The six look like this:

CC>CD>DC>DD
CC>DC>CD>DD
CC>DC>DD>CD
DC>CC>CD>DD
DC>CC>DD>CD
DC>DD>CC>CD

Not all of these are troublesome. If defection is bad all around,
everyone will avoid it. For a true dilemma to exist, there must be a
temptation to defect - otherwise, why defect?

In the prisoner's dilemma, there is every temptation to defect. No
matter what the other player does, you are better off defecting. The
temptation need not be that acute to pose a dilemma. You may have a
hunch what the other player is going to do, and know it is in your
advantage to defect provided the hunch is right. This could cause you
to defect, even though there may be no incentive to defect if your
hunch is wrong.

We require, then, that either of two conditions be met. Either there
is an incentive to defect when the other player cooperates (DC>CC), or
there is an incentive to defect when the other player defects (DD>CD)
- or both.

This rules out two of the games above. With the payoffs ordered
CC>CD>DC>DD or CC>DC>CD>DD, there is no incentive to defect at all.
Not only is mutual cooperation the best possible outcome, but a player
is guaranteed to do better by cooperating, no matter what the other
player does.

Crossing these two games off the list leaves just four games. Each is
important enough to rate a name.

DC>DD>CC>CD Deadlock
DC>CC>DD>CD Prisoner's Dilemma
DC>CC>CD>DD Chicken
CC>DC>DD>CD Stag Hunt

All four are common games in real-life interactions. For that reason
they are called "social dilemmas." All are closely related, too. Each
of the other three games can be derived from the prisoner's dilemma by
switching two of the payoffs in the order of preference. You can think
of the prisoner's dilemma as a center of gravity around which the
others orbit. Chicken is a prisoner's dilemma with punishment and
sucker payoffs reversed. The stag hunt is the prisoner's dilemma with
the preferences of the reward and temptation payoffs switched.
Deadlock is a prisoner's dilemma with the reward and punishment
payoffs switched.

ASYMMETRIC GAMES

The social dilemmas described above [Deadlock, Stag Hunt] are
symmetric games in which both players share the same preferences.
Preferences need not match, however. It is possible for one player's
preferences to be those of a prisoner's dilemma and the other player's
preferences to be those of chicken or stag hunt or something else.
Some of these hybrid games have been suggested as models for human
conflicts.

The game of bully is a cross between chicken and deadlock. One player
has the same preferences as a chicken player. He would like to defect,
but fears mutual defection. The other player has the deadlock
preferences and prefers to defect no matter what (preferably with the
other player cooperating). These two sets of preferences describe a
game that looks like this:

Deadlock Player:
Cooperate Defect
Chicken Player: Cooperate 2,1 1,3
Defect 3,0 0,2

One instance of bully is the biblical tale demonstrating the wisdom of
King Solomon (1 Kings 3:16-28). Two women claim the same child as
their own. One is the real mother, and the other is an impostor.
Solomon proposes splitting the child in two. Hearing this horrific
suggestion, one woman abandons her claim to the child. Solomon awards
the child to that woman. The real mother would love her child so much
she would give it up to save its life.

In other words, the true mother has the preferences of a chicken
player. The knife is poised over the child. The dilemma is whether to
stand firm (defect) or give in (cooperate). The real mother most wants
to prevail - to stand firm on her claim while the impostor backs down.
The worst outcome from the real mother's standpoint is for neither
woman to give in. Then the child is cut in two.

The impostor has deadlock preferences. She evidently would rather see
the child killed than have it go to her rival. The name "bully" tells
what happens. The deadlock player can be a bully and defect. The
chicken player is powerless to prevent this. The only thing she can do
is cut her losses by cooperating. Ergo, the woman who gives in is the
real mother.

Bully is a model for military confrontations in which one nation
prefers to start a war, and the other views the war as a catastrophe
to be avoided at all costs. To the extent this is an accurate model,
the conclusion is gloomy. The belligerent nation will likely get its
way, while the conciliatory nation is exploited to maintain the peace.
The prognosis is probably worse yet. Real nations' preferences are
fluid, and a nation that feels it has been exploited may decide that
war isn't so bad after all."

Ah, but you forget that there are 3 important factors that can drastically
alter the results of these basic models for Game Theory (Prisoner's Dilemma,
Stag Hunt, etc.)

1. Is it possible to determine if a player has defected?

2. If a player has defected, is there any way the other player can punish
him/her for the defection?

3. Is there repeated play?

of repeated play and the fact that repeated play doesn't necessarily have to be
with the same person to have the same effect here), the models (such as
Prisoner's Dilemma) aren't exactly accurate. This means that there is a much
higher cost of defecting (in general) and a much higher benefit of cooperating
(in general).

What do you gain beyond the gain you'd always get
from such a stab? Is it to "teach them a lesson" so
that they don't stab you as often in the future? Is
that even ethical? If your motive in stabbing is
something other than the immediate benefits, are you
really playing to win? (True, you're not required
to play to win in casual games, but I think most
players consider it unsportsmanlike to not play to
win even then.)

(If the stab helps you win, then sure you're playing
to win, but then why wouldn't you have stabbed
regardless of the stab you're exacting retribution
for? Does it damage your reputation among your
playgroup less if your stab is perceived to be
"retributive" or something?)

If we're talking about retaliating in games other
than the one where the original stab occurred, then
yes, I can see that you'll have more opportunities
to retaliate against people you play with regularly,
but I don't see how this is a good thing, or really
beneficial. If your point is that you can expect
the people you usually play with to keep their deals
more often because they know if they don't they'll
be subject to this kind of retaliation, that too
may be true but it feels kinda like blackmail to me
to threaten this and follow through on it.
